title: Security & Compliance: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, SDLC, Incident Response, Evidence Workflows and Exceptions
author: Ethan Park
content:
Overview

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's security and compliance controls and operational procedures across: RBAC and authentication, audit logging, data residency and retention, secure SDLC gates, incident response for security events, evidence collection workflows for compliance (SOC2/HIPAA/etc.), and risk/exception handling. It is intended for security, engineering, and compliance reviewers and provides operational checklists, ownership, thresholds, and sample config snippets.

Scope & Applicability

- Applies to hosted, dedicated, and private deployments, and to control-plane and data-plane components (API gateway, serving runtime, console, control plane services, CI/CD, and backup systems).
- Does NOT include customer application code hosted on customer-managed private deployments (see Private Deployments docs for customer responsibilities).

1) RBAC & Authentication

Goal: Ensure least-privilege access to systems and data, enforce strong authentication, and provide periodic access reviews.

Key controls:
- Centralized identity: SSO backed by SAML/OIDC (Okta for Redwood-managed accounts).
- Provisioning: SCIM for automated user provisioning and group membership.
- MFA: Enforced for all non-service accounts and for all admin/privileged roles (SMS/TOTP + hardware token for privileged access).
- Role model: Defined role registry (examples below).

Role registry (summary):
- security-admin: Full security team admin rights (lowest cardinality).
- infra-admin: Cloud and infra administration (limit to infra owners).
- platform-operator: Runtime/serving operational tasks (can access runtime metrics and logs, not customer PII).
- oncall-sre: Incident triage and mitigation privileges (time-limited elevated access via JIT).
- product-admin: Console feature flags and product config management (no direct PII export).

Access policies & examples:
- MFA required and policy enforced at IdP.
- Session lifetime: 8 hours for web console, 12 hours for device tokens; API keys limited to 90 days rotation recommended.
- JIT (Just-in-time) elevation: Temporary elevation via approval workflow recorded in audit logs.
- Privileged access review: Quarterly review for all members of infra-admin and security-admin groups.

Sample IAM (pseudo) policy snippet (for infra-admin):
- "AllowedActions": ["ec2:DescribeInstances","kms:Encrypt","kms:Decrypt"],
- "DenyActions": ["s3:GetObject:customer-data/*"],
- "Condition": {"SourceIp": "10.0.0.0/8"}  

Ownership:
- Identity & Access Management: security (policy) + eng-infra (implementation).
- Quarterly reviews: security (owner) with team leads as reviewers.

2) Audit Logging

Goal: Record a tamper-evident trail of access and actions across the control plane and data plane to support investigation, compliance evidence, and anomaly detection.

Log sources (minimum):
- API gateway (request/response metadata, client IPs, auth context)
- Inference runtime (request id, model version, top-level input sizes, output hashes for quality auditing)
- Console / Admin actions (changes to RBAC, rollouts, model pinning)
- CI/CD deploy events and artifact metadata (build ids, commits, authors)
- KMS/HSM access logs (Key usage events)
- Backup and restore operations

Log integrity & retention:
- Centralized log store: Splunk/Datadog/Elastic cluster with immutability for security-critical indices.
- Default retention: 365 days for control plane audit logs. High-sensitivity logs (privileged access, KMS events) retained 2 years by default for enterprise customers.
- Integrity: Logs are hashed on ingest (SHA-256) with periodic attestations and stored with read-only append-only policies.

Access controls on logs:
- Log access is RBAC controlled; separate roles for log readers vs log admins.
- Export of logs containing customer data requires approval and must be recorded as an evidence artifact.

Detection & alerting:
- Baseline alert rules: multiple failed authentication attempts (>5 in 5m), API key exfiltration heuristics (requests from new IP + large data export), privilege escalation events.
- Alert SLA: P1 alerts routed to security oncall immediately; P2 within 1 hour.

Example alert rule (pseudo):
- name: Privileged-Role-Add
- condition: event.type == "role_change" && event.new_role in ["security-admin","infra-admin"]
- notify: #security-oncall, create incident ticket

3) Data Residency & Retention

Principles:
- Customer data is stored only in customer-designated regions for Redwood-managed deployments. Cross-border transfer requires documented customer consent and legal review.
- Backups follow the same residency and encryption controls as primary data.

Default retention table (examples):
- Customer inference inputs/outputs: 30 days (default); configurable per-customer via contract.
- Audit logs (control plane): 365 days default; extendable to 2+ years for enterprise.
- Backups: 90 days snapshot rotation; snapshot metadata retained 2 years.
- Telemetry/metrics (aggregated): 13 months for historical trend analysis (no raw customer inputs).

Controls:
- Data-at-rest: AES-256 encryption via KMS. Customer-managed keys available for Private deployments (HSM integration).
- Data-in-transit: TLS 1.2+ enforced across all endpoints.
- Data classification: All data ingested is tagged at write-time with classification labels (customer-data, pii, telemetry, system).

Procedures for region changes or repatriation:
- Submit a written request to security and legal.
- Execute region data migration job with verification checksums and data destruction certificate for source region.
- Notify customer and record evidence in compliance evidence repo.

4) Secure SDLC (Software Development Life Cycle)

Gates and requirements for code that reaches production (applies to control plane services, runtime components, and infra-as-code):
- Threat modeling: Required for new services or major feature work (>2 sprints impact). Owner must complete STRIDE-based threat model stored in Confluence.
- Static analysis: Mandatory SAST for all repositories. Block pull requests with critical findings.
- Dependency management: SBOM maintained for each release. Vulnerable-high CVEs must be mitigated within 30 days or have an approved exception.
- Secret scanning: Prevent secrets in commits; any detected secrets trigger immediate rotation and incident process.
- CI/CD policy: All production deploys require passing unit/integration tests, SAST, and a security approval check.
- Runtime chaos & canary: New releases go to canary pool (5% traffic) with health checks and automated rollback on error-rate >1% or latency SLO breaches.

Pre-deploy checklist (for engineers):
1. Ensure PR passes automated checks (tests, linters, SAST).
2. Confirm SBOM updated and dependency audit clean or documented.
3. Document any new data flows and complete threat model (if applicable).
4. Schedule canary rollout and monitoring dashboards.
5. Obtain security review sign-off for high-risk changes.

Ownership:
- Secure SDLC policy: security (policy) + eng-developer-experience (tooling) + eng-infra (CI/CD enforcement).

5) Incident Response — Security Procedures

Purpose: Provide a repeatable process to detect, triage, contain, eradicate, recover, and communicate security incidents.

Severity definitions (high level):
- Sev1 (P1): Active data exfiltration, production compromise, or regulator-impacting breach.
- Sev2 (P2): Privilege escalation with limited scope, suspected but unconfirmed exfiltration.
- Sev3 (P3): Non-production incidents, minor misconfigurations, or low-risk vulnerability disclosures.

High-level process:
1. Detection & Alerting: Alerts escalate to security oncall. Use automated triage playbooks.
2. Triage: Determine scope, impacted systems, and data classification.
3. Containment: Isolate affected instances, revoke tokens/keys, rotate credentials.
4. Eradication: Apply fixes (patches, config changes), remove malicious artifacts.
5. Recovery: Restore services from known-good backups, monitor for recurrence.
6. Post-incident: Produce postmortem with timeline, root cause, mitigations, and lessons learned.

Required evidence collection during incidents:
- Preserve full audit logs for affected timeframe (export to evidence store).
- Snapshot affected hosts (forensic image) and preserve chain-of-custody.
- Record all communication and mitigations in incident ticketing system.

Notification timelines & legal engagement:
- Internal notification: security + affected service owners within 1 hour of detection for P1.
- Customer notification: follow contractual SLA and legal guidance; escalate to legal for regulatory timelines (e.g., GDPR 72-hour notification may apply).
- Regulatory reporting: security/legal determine obligations (SOC2, GDPR, HIPAA).

Runbook references and playbooks:
- On-call playbook: runbook for rotating keys, disabling accounts, isolating clusters, and emergency rollback.
- Forensic playbook: steps for imaging, log preservation, and evidence handoff to legal.

6) Compliance Evidence Workflows

Objective: Maintain an auditable evidence repository to support SOC2, ISO, HIPAA, and custom customer audits.

Evidence types and storage:
- Policies and procedures: Confluence (restricted space) with version history.
- System configurations and diagrams: Stored in versioned repo (architecture/diagrams) and linked to Confluence.
- Audit logs and exports: Immutable evidence bucket with access logging.
- Penetration test reports and remediation tracking: Stored in evidence repo with remediation tickets.
- Training records and access review logs: HR/Security evidence store.

Evidence request process (for auditors or customers):
1. Submit request via compliance-ticketing queue with scope and timeline.
2. Evidence owner acknowledges within 3 business days and provides delivery timeline.
3. Prepare redacted artifacts as needed; coordinate with legal for sensitive disclosures.
4. Deliver artifacts to auditor via secure file share; record delivery and receipt in evidence log.

Periodic evidence refresh:
- Quarterly: access reviews, training completion, and control attestations.
- Annually: full control re-evaluation for SOC2/ISO scope.

7) Risk & Exceptions

Handling exceptions to controls:
- Exception request: Submit an Exception Request Form with rationale, compensating controls, risk owner, and TTL (max 90 days without reapproval).
- Approval: Security + Service Owner + Legal (if required) must approve. High-risk exceptions require executive-level sign-off.
- Registry: Approved exceptions are tracked in the Risk & Exceptions register maintained by security.

Compensating controls examples:
- If a dependency cannot be patched immediately, require network isolation and additional monitoring with temporary WAF rules.
- If MFA cannot be enforced for a service account, restrict network source IPs and enforce short-lived credentials.

Renewal and closure:
- Exceptions must be re-evaluated at TTL expiry and closed when permanent remediation is implemented.

8) Roles & Ownership Matrix (summary)

- security: Policy author, incident response lead, compliance evidence owner.
- eng-infra: IAM implementation, infra hardening, backup and restore.
- eng-sre / platform: Runtime instrumentation, oncall, alerting rules.
- eng-developer-experience: SDLC automation, SAST, SBOM enforcement.
- legal & privacy: Regulatory interpretation, customer notification cadence.

Compliance Checklist (for audits / readiness)

- RBAC policies defined and enforced via IdP and cloud IAM.
- MFA enabled for all privileged users.
- Audit logging enabled and retention configured per policy.
- Data residency choices documented per customer and enforced.
- Secure SDLC gates in CI/CD and SBOM present.
- Incident playbooks exercised in the last 12 months (game day).
- Evidence artifacts prepared and stored in evidence repository with access controls.
- Exception register present and up-to-date.
